entries.focus: Likes and dislikes using familiar food vocabulary

video.title: Talking about food — Real Easy English

formatEvidence.method: Current official YouTube metadata, not URL shape or a thumbnail; no video downloaded

captionEvidence.source: Timed captions from the same official YouTube upload

factualCueSummaries.summary: Beth agrees and says she loves seafood.
Beth names baked beans as her least favourite food and expresses strong dislike.

questions.hint: Listen after Beth asks about his favourite food

questions.answer: Yes, she does. Beth loves seafood

questions.hint: Listen to her answer about her least favourite food
questions.answer: No, she doesn’t. Beth hates baked beans

questions.prompt: What food do you like? What food don’t you like? Ask your teacher, too
questions.hint: Use I like… and I don’t like… Then ask What about you?
questions.answer: Example: I like pizza. I don’t like fish. What about you?

entries.focus: Compare travel preferences and explain a change of mind

video.title: The First Guy To Ever Go Camping

formatEvidence.method: Current official YouTube metadata, not URL shape or a thumbnail; no video downloaded

captionEvidence.source: Timed captions from the same official YouTube upload

factualCueSummaries.summary: Camping is compared with a less comfortable version of their home setup; the hesitant man asks why they do not stay home.
His friend proposes disconnecting from comforts, houses and devices and reconnecting with nature.
The hesitant man says this sounds nice and agrees to go camping.

questions.prompt: Why does one man suggest staying at home?
questions.hint: Compare the camping equipment with what they already have at home
questions.answer: He thinks camping gives them a less comfortable version of what they already have at home

questions.prompt: What does his friend think they depend on too much?
questions.hint: Listen for three things before disconnect
questions.answer: His friend thinks they depend too much on their comforts, houses and devices

questions.prompt: What finally makes camping sound nice to the hesitant man?
questions.hint: Listen to the suggestion about nature and the stars
questions.answer: The idea of disconnecting from their usual comforts, reconnecting with nature and looking at the stars makes it sound nice

questions.prompt: Would you choose a camping trip or a comfortable hotel? Explain why and ask your teacher
questions.hint: Compare comfort, nature and being away from your devices
questions.answer: Example: I’d choose camping because I’d like to switch off and spend time outdoors. What would you choose?

entries.focus: Analyse work-life satire, distinguish available time from energy and negotiate a boundary

video.title: The First Guy To Ever Work In An Office

formatEvidence.method: Current official YouTube metadata, not URL shape or a thumbnail; no video downloaded

captionEvidence.source: Timed captions from the same official YouTube upload

factualCueSummaries.summary: The employee asks to decorate his cubicle; a family photograph is suggested as a reminder that work keeps him away from them for most waking hours.
The employee expects to be tired in the early morning and tired again after a full day of work.
Two days off are undercut by having energy for one activity and then recovering for the next week.

questions.prompt: What is ironic about the suggestion to display a family photograph?
questions.hint: Notice what the photograph is supposed to remind the employee of
questions.answer: The photograph is presented as decoration, but it reminds the employee that work keeps him away from his family for most of his waking hours

questions.prompt: Why don’t the proposed mornings and evenings resolve his concern?
questions.hint: Compare the available time with the energy he expects to have
questions.answer: He expects to be tired early in the morning and tired again after working all day, so available hours do not necessarily mean meaningful time with family and friends

questions.prompt: How does the sketch undermine the promise of two days off?
questions.hint: Listen to how much activity and recovery the speaker predicts
questions.answer: The speaker suggests he will have energy for about one activity and then need to recover before repeating the working week

questions.prompt: How would you challenge this proposal constructively and protect time outside work?
questions.hint: Name one concern and negotiate a concrete change, such as hours, commuting or availability
questions.answer: Example: I’m interested in the role, but the schedule leaves little energy for life outside work. Could we agree on flexible hours and clear limits on availability?
